title: Anthropic reinvents source control as Claude floods the world with code
source_used: The Register (read in full); facts cross-checked against Anthropic engineering blog "Redesigning source control at Anthropic"
key_facts: Anthropic published a blog post on Tuesday 13 Oct 2026 about Scion, an in-house version control system that replaced Git for its main code repository (monorepo).
Code changes merged per day rose from about 2,500 in May 2026 to over 30,000 as of September, according to Anthropic.

Anthropic's main branch history is about 100 GB, a compressed working copy is more than a quarter of that, and it runs about 25 million code checkouts a day for continuous integration (CI); fetched naively that would be over 600 PB of Git traffic per day.
Work on Scion started in January and the migration took five months; Claude also helped build Antique (a code review interface), a code search tool and a source control access-control system.
When Claude Mythos Preview became available internally, Anthropic had it rewrite an early Git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline; the result used 20 times less memory and ran four times as fast.
Anthropic says its engineers often had to tell Claude "no", because agents sometimes break core system constraints.
Anthropic says Scion is not right for general use and will not be released as open source; it expects other organisations to meet similar code-volume problems within months (The Register's account).
quote_evidence: In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day
Anthropic says its bespoke system isn't right for general use. There will be no open source release.
The much-hyped model produced a version that used 20 times less memory and ran four times as fast.
why_it_matters_hint: Managing AI-written code, not writing it, has become the bottleneck at Anthropic, and the company expects others to hit the same limit.
event_date: 13 Oct 2026 (Anthropic blog post); merge figures cover May to September 2026
notes: Numbers are Anthropic's own claims relayed by The Register; I also read Anthropic's original post (anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control), which matches The Register on the figures, the 20x/4x result and the five-month migration.
